stem: A product manager at a SaaS company has drafted 12 user stories for a new billing-export feature and wants to use Claude to improve them before sprint planning on Thursday. Which prompt makes the best use of Claude for requirements analysis?

options.text: Paste the stories and ask Claude to confirm that they are complete, unambiguous and ready for the sprint so the team can move straight to planning.
options.why: Asking for approval invites a confident yes. Claude cannot know what the team left out unless it is asked to look for gaps, and its agreement is not a sign-off.

options.text: Ask Claude to flag gaps, ambiguity and edge cases in each story and to propose testable acceptance criteria, marking any assumptions.
options.why: Claude adds most value as a critical reader: it surfaces what is unclear or missing and drafts acceptance criteria the team can then confirm or reject. Marking assumptions keeps invented details visible.

options.text: Paste the stories and ask Claude to rewrite them in more formal language.
options.why: Polishing the wording does not find missing scenarios or untestable requirements; the stories stay as incomplete as before, only more formal.

options.text: Paste the stories and ask Claude to assign story points so the team can skip estimation.
options.why: Estimation depends on the team's velocity, codebase and capacity, none of which Claude has. Numbers it produces would look precise but carry no information the team can plan on.

explanation: Use Claude to stress-test requirements: ask it to find gaps, ambiguity and edge cases and to draft acceptance criteria, with assumptions flagged. It is a reviewer and drafter, not an approver or an estimator of the team's own work.
reference: Claude Help Center — Get better results from Claude (clear, specific prompts); Exam guide Domain 4

stem: An HR lead wants to find which parts of new-hire onboarding are good candidates for Claude. She asks Claude "Which onboarding tasks should we automate?" and receives a generic list (send welcome email, schedule orientation, collect forms) that does not match how her team works. What should she do next to get a useful use-case analysis?

options.text: Ask the same question again with research mode turned on so Claude can search for published onboarding-automation case studies and best practices from HR consultancies and software vendors.
options.why: Web research returns what other organisations do in general. The missing input is her own process, which no search will find.

options.text: Ask Claude to rank the generic list by expected time saved and start with the top three.
options.why: Ranking a list that does not describe her process just adds false precision to the wrong candidates.

options.text: Accept the list, since onboarding is similar everywhere, and pick the three items that sound easiest.
options.why: Onboarding varies by systems, volumes and policies; choosing from a generic list skips the analysis the exercise was meant to do.

options.text: Describe her actual 22-step process, owners, volumes and pain points, and ask Claude to assess each step against explicit criteria such as volume, rule-basedness and error risk.
options.why: Claude can only analyse what it is given. Supplying the real process and explicit criteria turns a generic answer into a step-by-step assessment the team can act on and challenge.

explanation: Use-case analysis needs the real process as input: steps, owners, volumes, systems and pain points, plus the criteria for a good candidate (frequent, rule-based, low risk, drafting-heavy). Without that context Claude can only return textbook lists.
reference: Exam guide Domain 4 — Apply Claude to analyze requirements and use cases

stem: A consultant scoping an engagement for a regional retailer that wants "AI for customer service" has uploaded two discovery-call transcripts and asked Claude to draft a requirements document. Which two practices make the resulting analysis reliable enough to take back to the client? (Choose two.)

options.text: Ask Claude to separate requirements stakeholders stated explicitly from ones it inferred, and to list open questions for the next client meeting.
options.why: Keeping stated and inferred requirements apart, with open questions, makes Claude's contribution auditable and gives the consultant a concrete agenda for validation.

options.text: Treat everything in the document as confirmed, because it was generated from the client's own transcripts.
options.why: A transcript is a source, not a validation. Claude fills gaps with plausible inferences, and only the client can confirm them.

options.text: Ask Claude to add standard retail customer-service requirements the client did not mention and present them as client needs.
options.why: Presenting invented requirements as the client's own misrepresents what was said. Suggestions can be offered, but they must be labelled as the consultant's proposals.

options.text: Ask Claude to stress-test the draft for requirements that conflict, cannot be measured, or depend on information nobody has yet supplied.
options.why: A deliberate critique pass finds contradictions and untestable statements before the client sees them, which is where Claude adds value as a thinking partner.

options.text: Have Claude produce the final sign-off version so the client can approve it without another review cycle.
options.why: Requirements are a decision the client owns. Skipping their review to save a cycle is how misread needs become scope disputes.

explanation: When Claude drafts requirements from raw inputs, make its reasoning visible: separate stated from inferred, gather open questions, and run a critique pass for conflicts and unmeasurable statements. Confirmation stays with the stakeholders.
reference: Exam guide Domain 4 — Apply Claude to analyze requirements and use cases

stem: A project manager used Claude to turn workshop notes into a requirements document for a clinic scheduling tool. The document is polished, but the team notices acceptance criteria such as "the system should be fast" and "reminders should be sent promptly", and a section about "patient portal single sign-on" that nobody in the workshop mentioned. Regulatory sign-off requires testable criteria, and stakeholders review the document next week. What is the best next step?

options.text: Ask Claude to make the document more detailed and comprehensive before the review.
options.why: More detail from the same inputs produces more invented specifics. The problem is unverifiable and unsourced content, not a lack of length.

options.text: Send the document to stakeholders as it stands with a covering note asking them to read carefully and report anything that looks wrong, vague or unfamiliar before the regulatory review begins.
options.why: This shifts detection to busy reviewers who will skim, and the vague criteria would still fail the regulatory requirement for testability.

options.text: Supply the workshop notes and real targets, ask Claude to rewrite vague criteria as measurable ones and to flag any requirement it cannot trace to the notes for stakeholder confirmation.
options.why: This fixes both defects: vague criteria become testable using numbers the team owns, and untraceable content such as the SSO section is exposed rather than silently kept.

options.text: Regenerate the document with a more capable model, since the current one hallucinated a requirement.
options.why: Any model will fill gaps when the notes are silent. Traceability to sources is a process control, not something a model tier provides.

explanation: Two classic failures of AI-drafted requirements are unmeasurable criteria and content with no source. The remedy is to supply the real targets, ask for measurable rewrites, and require every requirement to trace back to an input, flagging the rest for humans to confirm.
reference: Exam guide Domains 2 and 4 — verification of outputs; requirements analysis

stem: A school administrator is using Claude to analyse requirements for a new after-school programme registration process. The school's data policy prohibits uploading student or parent names to Claude. The governing board requires that every requirement be traceable to a stakeholder input. Claude has already produced a first draft from an anonymised summary of a 180-response parent survey. Which action best advances the analysis while meeting every constraint?

options.text: Ask Claude to add a traceability column citing the survey question and anonymised respondent group behind each requirement, labelling unsourced items as assumptions.
options.why: Traceability to anonymised survey questions and groups satisfies the board without exposing names, and labelling unsourced items as assumptions keeps Claude's inferences honest.

options.text: Upload the raw survey export, including respondent names and email addresses, so Claude can trace each requirement to the specific parent who raised it and the board can contact them if needed.
options.why: This meets the traceability rule by breaking the data policy. Names are not needed for traceability; questions and groups are enough.

options.text: Ask Claude to rank the drafted requirements by importance and adopt the top ten for the board paper.
options.why: Prioritisation does not establish where each requirement came from, so the board's traceability requirement remains unmet.

options.text: Ask Claude to create representative parent personas and attribute each requirement to a persona.
options.why: Personas are fabricated stakeholders. Attributing requirements to them looks like traceability but traces to nothing real.

explanation: Traceability means linking each requirement to a real, citable input. Anonymised survey questions and respondent groups provide that link without breaching the data policy, and anything Claude inferred must be marked as an assumption rather than dressed up as a stakeholder need.
reference: Exam guide Domains 4 and 6 — requirements analysis; data sensitivity

stem: An operations manager needs a current overview of warehouse-management software vendors, including recent pricing tiers and customer reviews, for a decision meeting next week. Which approach best fits?

options.text: Ask Claude in a plain chat, without web search, to list the leading vendors, their pricing tiers and what customers say about them, since Claude has read widely about this market.
options.why: Without search Claude answers from training data, so pricing and product details may be out of date or wrong, with no sources to check.

options.text: Upload one vendor's brochure to a Project and ask Claude to compare it with the market.
options.why: One brochure gives Claude a single, self-interested source; it has nothing current about the other vendors to compare against.

options.text: Use research mode so Claude runs linked web searches and returns a cited report, then check the pricing claims against the vendors' own pages.
options.why: Research mode is built for multi-step investigation with citations. Verifying the figures that will drive the decision against primary sources is the diligence step.

options.text: Ask Claude to recall the latest analyst rankings for this software category.
options.why: Recalled rankings are unsourced and may be stale or fabricated, which is exactly what a decision meeting cannot rely on.

explanation: For current external information, research mode's agentic web searching with citations beats recall from training data. Citations make verification possible; the associate still checks the claims that matter.
reference: Claude Help Center — Use research on Claude

stem: An operations team receives about 300 vendor emails a week, and invoice queries take an average of four working days to answer. The team lead wants to use Claude to find where the delay comes from. Which approach is most likely to produce a useful bottleneck analysis?

options.text: Describe each step with owners, handoffs, volumes and waits, and ask Claude to map the process, find where work queues and propose measurable changes to validate with the team.
options.why: A process map built from real steps, volumes and waits lets Claude locate queues and handoffs, and proposing measurable changes gives the team something to test rather than adopt on faith.

options.text: Ask Claude "How can we speed up vendor email triage?" and implement its top suggestion.
options.why: Without the team's process, Claude can only offer generic advice that may target a step that is not the bottleneck.

options.text: Connect the shared Gmail inbox through the connector and ask Claude to start answering invoice queries directly, since removing the human step will shorten the four-day turnaround immediately.
options.why: Automating replies before understanding the flow may speed the wrong step and skips the analysis the lead asked for.

options.text: Ask Claude to draft a policy requiring vendors to phone instead of email for invoice questions.
options.why: Moving the channel does not remove the internal delay and is a decision, not an analysis.

explanation: Process optimisation with Claude starts with a faithful description of the current process: steps, owners, handoffs, volumes and waits. Claude can then map it, point to queues and suggest changes that the people who do the work validate.
reference: Exam guide Domain 4 — Leverage Claude for research, planning, and process optimization

stem: A consultant uses research mode to compile a briefing on new data-residency rules for a public-sector client. The brief will shape the client's procurement plan. Which two practices most improve the reliability of the research? (Choose two.)

options.text: Accept the report as final because research mode provides citations for its claims.
options.why: Citations make checking possible; they do not replace it. A cited source may be outdated, misread or about a different jurisdiction.

options.text: State the jurisdiction and the as-of date in the prompt, and ask Claude to flag where sources disagree or are older than the current rules.
options.why: Scoping the question and asking for disagreement and dates makes the report show its uncertainty instead of smoothing it over.

options.text: Ask Claude to remove the citations so the brief reads more cleanly for the client.
options.why: Stripping citations destroys the trail the client needs to verify claims that will shape spending.

options.text: Turn web search off and rely on Claude's training knowledge, since web results can be noisy.
options.why: Regulations change; training knowledge has a cutoff and no source dates, which is worse for a current-rules brief.

options.text: Check the claims the recommendation rests on against the regulator's primary text before the brief goes to the client.
options.why: Verifying the load-bearing claims against the authoritative source is the diligence step that turns a research draft into advice a client can act on.

explanation: Reliable research with Claude comes from a well-scoped prompt (jurisdiction, dates, ask for disagreements) plus verification of the claims that matter against primary sources. Citations are the starting point for checking, not a substitute for it.
reference: Claude Help Center — Use research on Claude; Exam guide Domain 2 (fact-checking)

stem: An operations lead asked Claude to analyse the vendor-invoice process using the team's written procedure and got a clear answer: the bottleneck is the finance approver. The team suspects the real delay is emails sitting unassigned in the shared inbox, which the procedure does not describe. The ticketing system can export anonymised timestamps for each step. Which next step gives the most trustworthy analysis?

options.text: Go with Claude's conclusion, since it is based on the documented procedure that the team itself wrote, and was stated confidently with a clear chain of reasoning.
options.why: Claude analysed the procedure as written, not the process as lived. Confidence reflects the clarity of the input, not its accuracy.

options.text: Ask Claude to reconsider and state which bottleneck it is most confident about.
options.why: Re-asking with the same inputs cannot reveal a step the inputs never mentioned; self-reported confidence adds nothing.

options.text: Interview the finance approver to confirm Claude's finding.
options.why: This tests only one hypothesis and ignores the unassigned-inbox suspicion that the procedure could never have surfaced.

options.text: Export the anonymised timestamps and ask Claude to compute wait time per step, including the unassigned period, then compare with the procedure-based view.
options.why: Measured wait times reveal where work actually waits, including steps missing from the procedure. Comparing data with the documented view is how the team learns which picture is true.

explanation: Claude's process analysis is only as good as the description it receives. When the documented process may not match reality, feed Claude measured data (timestamps, volumes) and compare the two views before acting.
reference: Exam guide Domain 4 — process optimization; Domain 2 — evaluate outputs for completeness

stem: A school administrator is planning the spring term with Claude. The plan must respect fixed exam windows, staffing rules and workload limits, and it will be regenerated at least three times as exam dates are confirmed. A union representative must be able to see which staffing rule each allocation satisfies before the plan is published, and the final version has to be loaded into the school's calendar system as a CSV. Which setup best supports this planning work?

options.text: Run a single long chat, paste the constraints each time dates change, and ask for the final plan in prose.
options.why: Re-pasting constraints invites drift between versions, and a prose plan gives the union representative no rule-by-rule view and produces no CSV.

options.text: Create a Project with the term dates, staffing rules and workload limits as knowledge, with instructions to output the plan as a table that shows the rule each allocation satisfies plus a CSV artifact, and regenerate in a new chat each time dates change, with the representative reviewing before publication.
options.why: Stable constraints live in the Project so every regeneration uses the same rules; the rule column gives the representative what they need; the CSV artifact meets the calendar requirement; and publication stays a human decision.

options.text: Use research mode to find other schools' published term plans and adapt the closest match.
options.why: Other schools' plans do not reflect this school's exam windows, staff or workload rules; the planning constraints are internal, not researchable.

options.text: Ask Claude to generate the plan and then, through the Google Calendar connector, create all the events directly so no CSV step is needed.
options.why: Writing events straight into calendars bypasses the union review the process requires and would have to be undone every time the dates move.

explanation: Planning work that repeats under stable constraints belongs in a Project: constraints as knowledge, output format in instructions, fresh chats for each regeneration. Showing which rule each decision satisfies keeps the human reviewers in control, and artifacts deliver the exportable format.
reference: Claude Help Center — What are projects?; What are artifacts and how do I use them?

stem: A marketing manager is designing a new content-approval workflow and wants to use Claude as a thinking partner. Which way of working keeps the design sound and the decision with the team?

options.text: Ask Claude to choose the best workflow and adopt it, since Claude is more objective than the team and has seen many approval workflows.
options.why: Claude does not know the team's politics, tooling or history; handing it the decision removes the judgement that only the people affected can supply.

options.text: Ask Claude for a single recommended design and roll it out without team review.
options.why: One unreviewed design skips the comparison of alternatives and the check against how the team really works.

options.text: Finish the design internally first and use Claude only to format the final document.
options.why: This wastes the point of a thinking partner, which is to generate and critique alternatives while the design is still open.

options.text: Ask Claude for two or three alternative designs with trade-offs, then critique and choose with the team.
options.why: Generating alternatives with trade-offs, then deciding and refining as a team, uses Claude for breadth and critique while keeping ownership with the humans.

explanation: As a solution-design partner, Claude is best used to widen the option set and surface trade-offs. The team compares, decides and iterates; Claude drafts and challenges but does not own the decision.
reference: Exam guide Domain 4 — Use Claude to support solution design, development, and iteration

stem: An HR team built a Project that answers new-hire questions from the employee handbook. In a test with 20 sample questions, 6 answers about benefits were wrong. What is the right way to iterate on the design?

options.text: Add "Always answer benefits questions correctly and double-check every benefits answer against the handbook before responding" to the project instructions and retest.
options.why: An instruction to be correct cannot supply facts the knowledge lacks or fix an outdated document; it changes nothing about the cause.

options.text: Look for a common cause behind the six failures, such as an outdated benefits document, fix it, and rerun the same 20 questions.
options.why: Diagnosing the pattern behind the failures targets the real defect, and rerunning the same test set shows whether the change worked without introducing new errors.

options.text: Rephrase the questions and rerun until all 20 pass, then launch.
options.why: Changing the questions until they pass tests nothing; new hires will ask in their own words.

options.text: Expand the test set to 200 questions before making any changes.
options.why: More failing examples of the same defect adds cost without diagnosis; fix the identified cause first, then widen the test.

explanation: Iteration means diagnosing the cause of failures, changing one thing that addresses it, and re-measuring on the same test set. Instruction pleading and test-rewriting are the tempting non-fixes.
reference: Exam guide Domains 4 and 7 — solution iteration; diagnosing poor outputs

stem: A product manager is designing a Claude-assisted process for triaging customer feedback at a retail bank. Which two practices best use Claude to strengthen the design before it is rolled out? (Choose two.)

options.text: Ask Claude whether the design is optimal and proceed once it agrees.
options.why: Claude tends to affirm a design it is asked to approve; agreement is not evidence.

options.text: Skip a pilot because the design worked on three example messages in the chat.
options.why: Three hand-picked examples say nothing about the variety of real feedback; small demos routinely hide failure modes.

options.text: Ask Claude to critique the design from the perspective of specific stakeholders, such as a frontline agent and the bank's privacy officer, to surface objections early.
options.why: Role-based critique is a cheap way to find operational and compliance objections before real stakeholders raise them.

options.text: Let Claude make the go/no-go decision based on its own assessment of the pilot.
options.why: The rollout decision weighs risk, resourcing and accountability, which belong to the PM and sponsors.

options.text: Pilot with 50 anonymised real feedback items, compare Claude's triage against human labels, and fix the design before scaling.
options.why: A small labelled pilot on real, anonymised data measures whether the design works and points to what to change.

explanation: Strengthen a design by having Claude critique it from concrete stakeholder viewpoints and by piloting on a labelled sample of real (anonymised) data. Approval-seeking, tiny demos and delegated go/no-go decisions are the traps.
reference: Exam guide Domain 4 — solution design and iteration; Domain 6 — data sensitivity

stem: A consultant has designed a process in which Claude classifies a retailer's product-return requests (about 2,000 a week) and drafts customer responses. The client now asks for approvals to be "fully automated". About 8% of returns show fraud indicators and must be judged by a person, the returns policy changes monthly, and the client has no developers and wants to run the process in Claude.ai this quarter. Which revised design satisfies every constraint?

options.text: Claude classifies and drafts; anything flagged for possible fraud or above a value threshold routes to a person; the current policy lives in Project knowledge and is replaced monthly; accuracy is measured on a labelled sample before automation widens.
options.why: This keeps human judgement where the risk is, keeps the policy current through a monthly refresh, works entirely in Claude.ai, and uses measurement to decide how far automation can safely go.

options.text: Automate approvals for every request as asked, with an instruction that Claude must never approve a fraudulent return.
options.why: An instruction cannot guarantee fraud detection; a probabilistic classifier auto-approving all requests violates the constraint that fraud cases be judged by a person.

options.text: Recommend that the client commission a developer-built integration with fraud scoring before proceeding.
options.why: Escalation to developers is right when a technical build is required, but the client's constraints (no developers, this quarter, Claude.ai) can be met with a Project and a human checkpoint.

options.text: Automate approvals for requests Claude classifies as non-fraud and route only the ones it flags to a person.
options.why: This trusts the classifier to catch every fraud case with no measured accuracy or value threshold; missed cases would be auto-approved.

explanation: Good solution design places Claude at the drafting and classification steps, keeps a human checkpoint where errors are costly, maintains the knowledge the process depends on, and expands automation only as measured accuracy justifies it.
reference: Exam guide Domain 4 — solution design; Domain 2 — determine when human review is required

stem: A project manager at a fintech ran a pilot in which Claude drafts responses to customer complaints. 92% of drafts were acceptable; almost all failures involved regulatory complaints, which must be answered within eight days by a compliance-trained agent. The pilot runs entirely in Claude.ai and can be adjusted this week. Which next iteration best fits the results and the constraints?

options.text: Extend the pilot to all complaint types and monitor the failure rate over the next month.
options.why: Scaling without addressing the known failure category exposes regulated complaints to the highest error rate.

options.text: Add "Regulatory complaints must be handled perfectly" to the instructions and rerun the pilot.
options.why: Emphatic wording does not give Claude the compliance judgement the failures show it lacks; the design, not the tone, needs to change.

options.text: Add a first step in which Claude classifies each complaint and routes regulatory ones to compliance agents, then re-measure the failing category and keep a person as the final sender.
options.why: The results say Claude drafts well except for one category, so the design should route that category to the trained humans, measure again, and keep human sign-off on every outbound response.

options.text: Pause the pilot and ask the developer team to build an API pipeline with automated compliance checks.
options.why: Escalation is warranted when the need is technical, but the pilot's problem is a routing decision that can be made inside Claude.ai now.

explanation: Iterate on what the data shows: isolate the failing category with a classification-and-routing step, keep humans on the high-stakes path, re-measure that category, and preserve the human sender. Neither scaling nor stronger wording addresses the identified weakness.
reference: Exam guide Domain 4 — solution design and iteration; Domain 2 — human review

stem: An operations team handles about 300 vendor emails a week in five steps: read, classify (invoice, query, complaint, other), route to an owner, draft a reply, send. Where should the team integrate Claude first?

options.text: At classify and draft-reply, with a team member reviewing the classification and draft before anything is sent.
options.why: Classifying and drafting are repetitive language tasks where Claude adds clear value, and a human checkpoint before sending keeps errors from reaching vendors.

options.text: At the send step, by giving Claude permission through the Gmail connector to send replies as soon as they are drafted, without review.
options.why: Automating the irreversible step first removes the checkpoint that catches misclassifications and wrong drafts.

options.text: By replacing the whole five-step process with one Claude conversation per email.
options.why: Replacing the workflow discards the routing and ownership the team relies on; augmentation at specific steps is the lower-risk start.

options.text: Only at the end of the week, to write a summary report of email volumes.
options.why: A weekly summary is useful but leaves the daily drafting and classifying load, where the time goes, untouched.

explanation: Integrate Claude at the steps where it adds the most value with the least risk (classifying, summarising, drafting) and keep a human checkpoint before external or irreversible actions.
reference: Exam guide Domain 4 — Integrate Claude into existing workflows to augment or redesign them

stem: An HR team wants to bring Claude into its onboarding process. New hires currently ask coordinators dozens of policy questions, and coordinators write a personalised welcome pack for each hire by hand. Which integration augments the process appropriately?

options.text: Have Claude answer all new-hire questions, including contract, pay and benefits queries, so coordinators no longer need to be involved in day-to-day onboarding questions at all.
options.why: Pay and contract answers carry legal and financial consequences; removing HR from those questions puts probabilistic answers in a place that needs accountable ones.

options.text: Wait until Claude can be connected directly to the HR information system before changing anything.
options.why: Drafting packs and first-line policy answers need only the handbook and templates; delaying for a system integration forgoes value that is available now.

options.text: Use a Project with the handbook and pack template so Claude drafts welcome packs and answers first-line policy questions, with coordinators verifying pay, benefits and legal answers.
options.why: Drafting and first-line answers are where Claude saves time; routing consequential topics to coordinators keeps the human checkpoint where it matters.

options.text: Ask Claude once to generate a generic onboarding checklist and stop there.
options.why: A one-off checklist does not touch the recurring drafting and question load that consumes the coordinators' time.

explanation: Augmenting a workflow means placing Claude at the drafting and first-line steps with the right reference material, while keeping humans responsible for answers with legal, financial or contractual weight.
reference: Claude Help Center — What are projects?; Exam guide Domain 4

stem: A marketing team is integrating Claude into its weekly content pipeline (brief, draft, fact check, edit, approve, publish). Which two practices reflect good workflow integration? (Choose two.)

options.text: Define which step Claude owns (the first draft from a brief), which steps stay human (fact check, final approval), and the handoff format between them.
options.why: Clear ownership and handoffs are what make the integration repeatable; everyone knows what Claude produces and what a person must still do.

options.text: Require every writer to use Claude for every piece, regardless of the task.
options.why: Mandating use where it does not help breeds workarounds; integration should follow where Claude adds value.

options.text: Remove the editor's review step because Claude can check its own drafts.
options.why: Self-review by the same model is not independent verification; the editor is the checkpoint that catches errors and off-brand copy.

options.text: Measure time per piece and number of revision rounds for four weeks before and after, so the effect can be shown.
options.why: Baseline and post-change measurement turns "it feels faster" into evidence that supports or corrects the integration.

options.text: Connect Claude to the CMS so drafts are published as soon as they are generated.
options.why: Publishing straight from generation skips fact check and approval, the steps that protect the brand.

explanation: Good integration assigns Claude a specific step, preserves human checkpoints for verification and approval, defines handoffs, and measures the effect. Mandates, removed reviews and auto-publishing are the common mistakes.
reference: Exam guide Domain 4 — workflow integration; Domain 7 — optimize workflows

stem: An operations team on a Team plan has the Gmail connector enabled by an Owner and wants Claude to handle vendor emails asking about invoice status. About 12% of those emails concern disputed invoices that need a finance decision, and company policy requires a person to approve every outbound vendor communication. By default the connector asks for approval before Claude sends an email. Which integration satisfies all of these constraints?

options.text: Ask the Owner to allow send actions to run without asking, so Claude can reply to status queries as they arrive.
options.why: Removing the approval prompt breaks the policy requirement that a person approves every outbound vendor communication.

options.text: Let Claude send replies automatically only for emails it classifies as non-disputed, and forward the rest to finance.
options.why: This still sends unapproved emails, and any misclassified dispute would get an automatic answer; it violates the policy and trusts the classifier blindly.

options.text: Ask the developer team to build a custom integration that sends replies from a shared service mailbox without the approval step, so the connector's prompt no longer slows the team down.
options.why: Engineering around the approval control does not satisfy the policy; it just hides the violation in a different tool.

options.text: Have Claude classify and draft, route disputed invoices to finance, and keep the per-send approval so a team member reviews each reply before it goes out.
options.why: Classification and drafting take the effort out of the step; routing disputes to finance and keeping the approval prompt satisfy both the finance-judgement and human-approval constraints.

explanation: Connectors let Claude read and draft with live data, but actions such as sending email should keep the human approval that policy requires. Design the workflow so Claude does the drafting and routing and people keep the decision.
reference: Claude Help Center — Use Google Workspace connectors (approval before actions; owner controls on Team and Enterprise)

stem: A public-sector benefits office processes about 5,000 applications a month and a manager wants to redesign the intake workflow around Claude. Eligibility decisions must by law be made by a caseworker, many applicants submit scanned handwritten forms, and the budget committee will fund a rollout only after a pilot shows measured impact. Which two elements belong in the redesigned workflow? (Choose two.)

options.text: Claude issues eligibility decisions for straightforward cases so caseworkers can focus on complex ones.
options.why: The law places every eligibility decision with a caseworker; automating even simple decisions breaks that constraint.

options.text: Claude summarises each application and pre-fills a structured checklist of missing documents, which the caseworker verifies before deciding.
options.why: Summarising and pre-filling are exactly the augmentation steps where Claude saves caseworker time while the decision remains with the person.

options.text: Treat Claude's reading of handwritten scans as reliable enough to skip manual checking of extracted details.
options.why: Extraction from handwriting is error-prone; details that feed a legal decision need a verification step, not blind trust.

options.text: Stop the pilot and hand the whole project to developers to build a fully automated pipeline first.
options.why: Escalation to developers may come later, but the committee needs pilot evidence now, and a fully automated pipeline would conflict with the caseworker requirement.

options.text: Run a four-week pilot with a comparison group, measuring processing time and error rate, with caseworker sign-off retained throughout.
options.why: A measured pilot with a comparison group produces the evidence the committee requires while keeping the legal safeguard in place.

explanation: Redesigning a workflow around Claude still means augmenting the steps where it adds value (summarising, extracting, pre-filling) with verification, keeping legally required human decisions, and proving impact with a measured pilot before scaling.
reference: Exam guide Domain 4 — augment or redesign workflows; Domain 6 — appropriate use

stem: A consultant is presenting to a retailer's executive team on what Claude can do for the customer-service function. Which statement is accurate and sets the right expectation?

options.text: "Once we upload our policies, Claude's answers will always be accurate."
options.why: Reference documents improve grounding, but Claude can still misread, omit or invent details; accuracy is never guaranteed.

options.text: "Claude learns from every conversation, so the more staff use it the more accurate it becomes about our business, our products and our customers' history."
options.why: Claude does not retrain on a company's chats; memory can carry context between conversations, but it is not a learning system that improves accuracy over time.

options.text: "Claude speeds up drafting, summarising and analysis, but its output is probabilistic, so facts and decisions still need human checks."
options.why: This states the value honestly alongside the core limitation, which is the expectation executives need before funding a rollout.

options.text: "Claude guarantees our replies comply with consumer-protection law."
options.why: No model guarantees legal compliance; compliance remains a human responsibility supported by review processes.

explanation: Communicating value means pairing the concrete gains (drafting, summarising, analysis) with the honest limits: outputs are probabilistic, need verification, and do not carry guarantees of accuracy or compliance.
reference: Exam guide Domain 4 — Communicate Claude's value and limitations to stakeholders

stem: After a six-week onboarding pilot, the head of HR asks an associate: "Can Claude replace two of our four onboarding coordinators?" The pilot data show drafting time down 60%, review time unchanged, and 1 in 8 drafts needing a factual correction before use. What is the best response?

options.text: Say yes, since a 60% saving on drafting justifies halving the team and secures sponsorship for the rollout.
options.why: The 60% applies to one task, not to the coordinators' whole role; a headcount claim the data do not support will fail and damage trust.

options.text: Present the measured results, explain that drafting got faster while review load stayed the same and corrections are still needed, and recommend redeploying the saved time before drawing any headcount conclusions.
options.why: This is evidence-based, honest about the remaining review work and error rate, and steers the stakeholder to a decision the data can support.

options.text: Say the impact cannot be measured yet and suggest extending the pilot indefinitely.
options.why: The pilot did produce measurements; refusing to interpret them withholds useful information from the decision-maker.

options.text: Report only the 60% drafting improvement, since the correction rate would undermine confidence in the project.
options.why: Omitting the correction rate misrepresents the results and sets the stakeholder up to discover the limitation later, at higher cost.

explanation: Communicate value with the measured evidence, including the parts that limit the story (unchanged review load, error rate). Recommend conclusions the data support and avoid promises they do not.
reference: Exam guide Domain 4 — Communicate Claude's value and limitations to stakeholders

stem: A school administrator is briefing the governing board on a proposal to use Claude for parent communications and term planning. Which two points should the briefing include when explaining Claude's limitations? (Choose two.)

options.text: Claude can produce fluent text that contains incorrect facts, so anything published to parents will be checked by a staff member.
options.why: Naming the hallucination risk together with the verification control is the honest, actionable way to present the limitation.

options.text: Claude gives the same answer every time to the same prompt, so outputs can be approved once and reused.
options.why: Outputs vary between runs; approving one output does not certify future ones.

options.text: The school's data policy determines what may be uploaded, so student and parent personal data will be kept out of prompts and knowledge files unless the policy and plan allow it.
options.why: Data handling is a core limitation stakeholders need to understand; stating the rule and how it will be applied builds justified confidence.

options.text: Claude has real-time knowledge of all current education regulations.
options.why: Claude's knowledge has a cutoff and it does not monitor regulations; current rules must be supplied or researched and verified.

options.text: Claude understands what students need, so teacher input into plans is no longer required.
options.why: Claude has no knowledge of the school's students beyond what it is told; teachers' judgement remains essential.

explanation: An honest limitations briefing covers the probabilistic nature of outputs (with the verification step that manages it) and the data-handling rules the organisation will follow. Claims of determinism, real-time regulatory knowledge or replacing professional judgement are misrepresentations.
reference: Exam guide Domains 4 and 6 — communicate limitations; data sensitivity

stem: A marketing director wants to tell clients that the agency's brand-voice Project "knows our brand guidelines and never goes off-brand". The Project holds the guidelines as knowledge, and in a pilot 4 of 50 drafts needed voice edits before use. The legal team requires client-facing claims to be accurate. How should the associate advise the director to describe the Project?

options.text: Keep the claim, since 46 of 50 drafts is close enough to "never" for marketing purposes, and clients will understand that marketing language is not meant to be taken literally.
options.why: An 8% edit rate contradicts "never"; the claim fails the legal accuracy requirement and will be disproved by the first off-brand draft a client sees.

options.text: Drop any mention of Claude to avoid making claims about it at all.
options.why: Hiding the tool is unnecessary and prevents the agency from communicating a real, measurable benefit.

options.text: Say the Project "is trained on our brand guidelines" instead of "knows" them.
options.why: The guidelines are reference material in Project knowledge; Claude is not trained on them, so this wording is inaccurate in a different way.

options.text: Describe it as using the guidelines as reference material for drafts that editors review, citing that 92% of pilot drafts needed no voice edits.
options.why: This describes the mechanism correctly, keeps the human review visible, and uses the measured result as the evidence for the claim.

explanation: Stakeholder-facing claims should describe what the configuration does (reference material plus instructions), keep the review step visible, and use measured results rather than absolutes such as "never" or inaccurate mechanisms such as "trained on".
reference: Claude Help Center — What are projects?; Exam guide Domain 4

stem: A consultant is preparing the value statement for a public-sector client's Claude pilot. Procurement rules require that benefit claims be evidence-based and that limitations be documented. The pilot measured a 35% reduction in time to draft case summaries but did not measure any change in decision quality, and decisions remained with staff throughout. The client's communications team wants to announce "AI-driven decision-making that improves outcomes". Which value statement satisfies the constraints?

options.text: State the 35% drafting-time reduction with the method used to measure it, note that decision quality was not measured and that all decisions remained with staff, and document the limitations and data-handling rules that applied.
options.why: Every claim is backed by evidence, the unmeasured area is stated rather than implied, and the limitations are documented as procurement requires.

options.text: Adopt the communications team's framing, since the pilot involved staff who make decisions.
options.why: "AI-driven decision-making" is false (staff made the decisions) and "improves outcomes" is unmeasured, so it fails the evidence rule.

options.text: Report the 35% saving and infer that faster summaries mean better decisions.
options.why: Inferring a quality improvement from a speed measurement presents an assumption as evidence.

options.text: Delay any value statement until decision quality has been measured in a second pilot.
options.why: An evidence-based statement is possible now; the rules require honesty about what was measured, not silence until everything is.

explanation: Evidence-based value communication reports what was measured and how, states plainly what was not measured, and keeps the human role visible. It resists both overclaiming and unnecessary silence.
reference: Exam guide Domain 4 — Communicate Claude's value and limitations to stakeholders
